attributes.attribute: a fifth, used for the ancient provinces of Ireland
cosmological concept of the true center

sources: Aitchison, N. B. Armagh and the Royal Centres in Early Medieval Ireland: Monuments, Cosmology and the Past. Rochester, N.Y.: Crithne Press/Boydell & Brewer, 1994, 114.
Dames, Michael. Mythic Ireland. London: Thames and Hudson, 1992. Pp. 14-16.
Rees, Alwyn, and Brinley Rees. Celtic Heritage: Ancient Tradition in Ireland and Wales. London: Thames and Hudson, 1998, 118+.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Ancient Ireland divided into five regions. The term cóiced means a fifth. The four main ones were Leinster at the east, Munster at the southwest, Connacht at the west, and Ulster at the north. The fifth region, Mide or Meath, was not geographical. It was a cosmological concept that represented the true center. The center was sometimes defined as the hill of Uisneach. Later the five provinces were reduced to the four that remain today.

okr.objective: Explain the five provinces of ancient Ireland.
key_results: Explains Mide as the cosmological fifth province and true center
